questions.q: What is the primary setting of Meera Bai's poem "Mere to Giridhar Gopal" — a physical location or an internal state? Answer in one sentence.
questions.a: The primary setting is the speaker's internal spiritual consciousness centred on Krishna, not a physical place. A wrong answer naming Vrindavan, Chittor, or a temple reveals the student is confusing the poem's *references* to places with its actual metaphorical setting, a common error when students treat devotional poetry as narrative history.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the line "valqou ty lhafp&lhafp, izse&csfy cks;h" (tears flow continuously, night passes in separation) contributes to the poem's atmosphere.
questions.a: The line establishes an atmosphere of relentless, physicalised longing — the repetition "lhafp&lhafp" mimics unending tears, and "izse&csfy cks;h" stretches time into an endless night of separation, making the reader feel the visceral weight of viraha. A wrong answer that merely translates the line or calls it "sad" shows the student cannot connect linguistic choices (reduplication, time dilation) to emotional effect.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "metaphorical setting" to the phrase "esjs rks fxjèkj xksiky" (Giridhar Gopal is my only support). What does this declaration do to the poem's spatial coordinates?
questions.a: It collapses all external geography into a single relational coordinate: the speaker exists only in relation to Krishna. The setting becomes a dyadic space — wherever Krishna is, that is the speaker's world. A wrong answer describing it as "Meera saying she likes Krishna" misses the spatial reorientation and treats the line as emotional expression rather than setting construction.

questions.q: Compare the atmosphere of the first half of the poem (lines describing separation and helplessness) with the second half (lines describing union and fearlessness). What structural shift in atmosphere occurs?
questions.a: The atmosphere shifts from anxiety-ridden viraha (marked by "nirbal", "dukh", "bhay", endless night) to fearless fulfilment (marked by "sahaj", "anand", "abhay", "prem") — a movement from duality to non-duality where the devotee's identity merges with the beloved. A wrong answer listing separate emotions without noting the structural arc from separation to union misses the poem's architectural design.

questions.q: Evaluate this claim: "The poem's atmosphere is created mainly through its rhyme scheme and meter." Defend or refute with evidence from the text.
questions.a: Refute. While the folk meter (chhand) and rhyme support musicality, the atmosphere is primarily built through concrete imagery (tears, night, fire, rain), kinetic verbs (flow, pass, burn, drench), and direct address ("nkfl ehjka yky fxjèkj!") that pulls the listener into the speaker's immediate experience. A student agreeing with the claim reveals a formalist misconception that sound alone creates mood, ignoring the semantic and imagistic density of Braj Bhasha.

questions.q: Write a four-line stanza in Hindi (or Hinglish) that creates an atmosphere of *peaceful surrender* using the same metaphorical setting (inner landscape centred on the divine). Use at least two sensory images.
questions.a: Example: "man mandir mein deep jale, / swami tum hi ujiyare / sankalp vikalp sab mit gaye, / ab tum hi hamare." A poor answer that writes a generic prayer without sensory images (light, darkness, dissolution) or that describes an external temple instead of the inner landscape shows the student cannot transfer the concept of metaphorical setting to original creation.
